why_how.text: Driving is a legal privilege, so North Carolina ties it to holding a valid license and sets clear limits for learners.
A permit is a supervised stage: it names the vehicle, must be carried, and needs a licensed companion beside you.

scenario.text: Morgan, age nineteen, has a car learner permit and a licensed sister ready to ride in the front passenger seat.

reasoning.text: Morgan is old enough for a regular permit, and a licensed person seated beside Morgan meets the highway supervision rule.

result.text: Morgan may practice in the kind of car the permit names, as long as the permit is in Morgan's possession.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a permit holder may drive alone when there is little other traffic around.

correction.text: A permit holder on the highway always needs a person licensed for that vehicle seated alongside; only a licensed driver may drive alone.

memory_support.text: Permit has company, license drives alone.

prompt.text: Morgan has a learner permit and a licensed companion but left the permit at home. Can Morgan practice today?

answer.text: No. A learner permit only gives permission while it is in the holder's possession.

rationale.text: The age and companion rules are met, but the permit itself must be carried every time Morgan drives.

lines.text: A learner permit is where you start.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson of the North Carolina driver handbook. Before you learn a single road rule, the state sets the ground floor: driving on public streets and highways is a legal privilege, and it comes with responsibility. That privilege starts with a valid driver license. In this lesson you will see what counts as driving without one, who can get a regular learner permit, what that permit lets you do, and who has to sit beside you while you practice. By the end you should be able to tell a permit holder's limits apart from a licensed driver's freedom to drive alone.

lines.text: No valid license, no driving on public roads.
No sitting at the wheel with the engine running.
No steering a vehicle being pushed or towed.

narration.text: Here is the baseline rule. In North Carolina it is illegal to drive a motor vehicle on public streets and highways unless you hold a valid driver license. The handbook then closes two gaps that people sometimes overlook. Without a valid license you may not sit behind the wheel while the engine is running, even if the car is not moving. And you may not steer a vehicle while another vehicle pushes or tows it. So driving is broader than pressing the gas pedal. If a practice question describes someone unlicensed at the wheel of a running car, the answer is that it is not allowed.

lines.text: Drives only the vehicle class it names.
Works only while you carry it.

narration.text: Now the starting credential. A regular learner permit is available to anyone who is eighteen years old or older. The permit is narrow on purpose. It lets its holder drive the type or class of vehicle the permit names, and nothing else, and only while the permit is actually in the holder's possession. Leaving it at home means the permission stays at home too. To earn a permit you pass a vision check, a traffic signs test and a test on motor vehicle laws, which the next lesson covers in detail. For now, remember three limits: the right age, the named vehicle, and the permit on you.

lines.text: Permit: a licensed person seated beside you.

narration.text: This is where learners slip. When a permit holder drives on the highway, a person licensed for that vehicle must ride in the seat beside them. Not in the back seat, and not in another car following behind, but right alongside the driver. A licensed driver, by contrast, may drive alone. The tempting wrong answers on practice questions usually sound reasonable, such as any adult passenger, or no one at all if the permit holder is careful. Neither is enough. The companion must be licensed for that vehicle and seated beside the permit holder. Tie supervision to the permit, and driving alone to the license.

lines.text: Morgan left the permit at home.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Morgan is nineteen, holds a learner permit for a passenger car, and has a licensed sister ready to ride in the front passenger seat. But Morgan left the permit on the kitchen table. Can Morgan practice driving today? Work it through before reading on. The answer is no. A learner permit works only while it is in the holder's possession, so a permit left at home gives no permission on the road. If Morgan goes back for it, the rest of the plan is fine: Morgan is old enough for a regular permit, and a licensed sister seated beside Morgan meets the supervision rule.

lines.text: Permit at eighteen, carried, for the named vehicle.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Driving on North Carolina public streets and highways requires a valid driver license, and without one you may not even sit at the wheel with the engine running or steer a vehicle that is being pushed or towed. A regular learner permit is open to anyone eighteen or older. It covers only the vehicle class it names, only while you carry it, and on the highway a person licensed for that vehicle must sit beside you. A licensed driver may drive alone. Next, we look at the tests that stand between you and that permit or license.

why_how.text: The permit tests check that you can see, read signs and know the laws before you practice on the road.
An original license can add the on-road test, and every test is scored on its own, so no strong result covers a weak one.

scenario.text: Riley passes the vision check and the traffic signs test but misses the motor vehicle laws test.

reasoning.text: Each license test is scored separately, so the good signs result does not carry over to the laws test.

result.text: Riley must pass the laws test before getting a learner permit.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing the signs test and the knowledge test are the same exam with two names.

correction.text: The signs test is about identifying signs by color and shape and giving their meaning; the knowledge test covers traffic laws and safe driving practices.

prompt.text: Riley passed vision and signs but failed the laws test. Can Riley get a learner permit yet?

answer.text: Not yet. Riley must pass the laws test too.

rationale.text: A learner permit needs all three tests passed, and each test is scored on its own.

lines.text: Permits and licenses both start with tests.
Each test stands on its own.

narration.text: In this lesson we look at the tests that stand between you and driving. North Carolina uses a small set of tests, and which ones you face depends on whether you are applying for a learner permit or an original driver license. You will learn the three permit tests, the extra test an original license can add, why each test is passed separately, and how the signs test differs from the knowledge test. Knowing exactly what each test measures helps you study the right material, and it also helps on practice questions that try to swap one test for another.

lines.text: A test on motor vehicle laws.

narration.text: To get a learner permit, you must pass three things. First, a vision check, so the division knows you can see well enough to drive. Second, a traffic signs test. Third, a test on motor vehicle laws. Notice what is not on the list: the on-road driving test. A permit is the stage where you learn to drive, so the state does not ask you to prove driving skill yet. A simple way to hold the list is eyes, signs and laws. If a practice question offers the road test as a permit requirement, that option is the one to rule out.

Applicants for any original driver license may be tested on four areas: vision, knowledge of motor vehicle laws, traffic signs, and driving skill in an on-road test. And here is a rule that applies to every one of them. Each driver license test is scored on its own, so you must pass each one separately. A perfect signs score does not rescue a failed knowledge test, and scores are never averaged together. Treat each test as its own gate. You walk through one gate at a time, and every gate has to open before the license does.

lines.text: License: those plus the road test.

narration.text: Practice questions often blur these two lists, so keep them side by side. The learner permit tests are vision, signs and motor vehicle law knowledge. An original license can also require the on-road driving skill test. That road test is the difference. When a question asks which test a permit does not need, the answer is the road test. When a question asks what an original license applicant may face, the full list includes vision, laws, signs and driving skill. A distractor that puts the road test on the permit list, or leaves it off the license list, should stand out right away.

lines.text: Knowledge: traffic laws and safe practices.

narration.text: Two of the tests sound alike, but they ask different things. On the signs test you must recognize each traffic sign by its color and shape and give its meaning, and every sign that appears on that test is shown in the handbook, so studying the handbook signs is the direct route. The knowledge test covers traffic laws and safe driving practices. If reading is hard for you, an audio version of the knowledge test can be requested. So the signs test is about recognizing what you see, and the knowledge test is about the rules and habits of safe driving.

Here is a quick check: Riley is applying for a learner permit. Riley passes the vision check and does very well on the traffic signs test, but misses the motor vehicle laws test. Can Riley get the learner permit yet? Work it out before reading on. The answer is not yet. A learner permit needs all three tests, vision, signs and laws, and each driver license test is scored on its own. The strong signs result does not make up for the laws test. Riley needs to pass the laws test, and then the permit is within reach. Every gate opens on its own.

lines.text: License may add the road test.

narration.text: Here is the map to keep. A learner permit requires a vision check, a traffic signs test and a test on motor vehicle laws. An original driver license may test vision, law knowledge, signs and on-road driving skill. Every test is scored on its own, so each one must be passed separately. The signs test asks you to recognize signs by color and shape and give their meaning, while the knowledge test covers traffic laws and safe driving practices, with an audio version available on request. Next, we look at the vision check more closely and at fitness to drive.

why_how.text: Vision is checked at every in-person application, because safe driving starts with seeing the road.
A corrective-lens restriction is binding, and the penalty for ignoring it matches driving with no license.

scenario.text: Jamie needs glasses to meet the vision standard and gets a license with a corrective-lens restriction.

reasoning.text: The restriction means the glasses must be worn every time Jamie drives, and driving without them is punished like driving unlicensed.

result.text: Jamie keeps a spare pair in the glove box and puts them on before every trip.

claim.text: Many people think a corrective-lens restriction is a gentle suggestion, like a reminder to clean the windshield.

correction.text: Driving without the required lenses is treated like driving unlicensed, not like a minor equipment fault.

prompt.text: Jamie's license carries a corrective-lens restriction. Jamie drives to the store without glasses. How is that treated?

answer.text: The same way as driving with no license at all.

rationale.text: The restriction is binding; driving without the required lenses carries the no-license penalty.

narration.text: This lesson is about the driver, not the car. North Carolina checks that you can see well enough to drive, and it asks whether any mental or physical condition could make your driving unsafe. You will learn when your vision is checked, what happens if you need glasses or contacts to pass, why the corrective-lens restriction is taken so seriously, and how the division treats conditions and disabilities. The theme running through all of it is simple. The state is not judging labels or diagnoses. It is asking one question: can this person drive safely?

Your vision is checked whenever you apply in person, whether that visit is for a learner permit, an original license or a renewal. It is not a one-time check at your first license. If you need glasses or contact lenses to meet the vision standard, two things follow. You must wear them every time you drive, not only at night or on long trips. And your license will carry a corrective-lens restriction, so any officer who checks your license can see the requirement. In short, if the lenses got you through the vision check, the lenses ride with you on every drive.

Here is the trap. Many learners assume that forgetting required glasses is a small slip, like a burned-out bulb or a dirty windshield. The handbook says otherwise. Driving without the corrective lenses your license requires is punished the same way as driving with no license at all. That is a serious penalty, and it reflects the idea that your license was only granted on the condition that you see clearly. So the restriction is not a suggestion. On practice questions, any option that treats it as a warning, a minor equipment fault or something to ignore when you feel fine is the wrong one.

lines.text: A disability can mean a restricted license.

narration.text: The division also looks at fitness to drive. A person whose mental or physical condition could make driving unsafe may be denied a license. But a disability does not automatically bar anyone from licensing. If the condition does not prevent safe driving, the person can get a restricted license, shaped around what they can do safely. So the deciding question is never whether a person has a condition or a disability. It is whether that condition keeps them from driving safely. Practice questions that claim any reported condition means automatic refusal are testing whether you know this distinction.

Here is a quick check: Jamie needed glasses to pass the vision check, so Jamie's license carries a corrective-lens restriction. One afternoon Jamie drives to the store without the glasses, feeling that the trip is short and the eyesight is good enough. How is that treated? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that it is treated the same way as driving with no license at all. The restriction is binding every time Jamie drives, how Jamie feels about the eyesight does not matter, and the short trip does not change the rule.

lines.text: Vision checked at every in-person visit.

narration.text: To wrap up, your vision is checked whenever you apply in person, for a learner permit, an original license or a renewal. If you need glasses or contacts to meet the standard, you wear them every time you drive and your license shows a corrective-lens restriction. Driving without them is punished the same way as driving with no license. A condition that could make driving unsafe may lead to denial, while a disability that does not prevent safe driving can still lead to a restricted license. Next, we turn to the on-road driving test itself.

why_how.text: The road test comes last because it checks real driving after the vision, signs and knowledge tests are behind you.
Examiners grade a long list of everyday skills, so the test rewards steady habits rather than one special trick.
The three-point turnabout has a fixed wheel pattern that is easy to remember and easy to grade.

scenario.text: Taylor must turn around on a narrow street during the road test, starting from the far right edge.

reasoning.text: Taylor checks traffic, signals left, creeps forward with the wheel left, then backs slowly with the wheel right, then moves forward with the wheel left.

result.text: Taylor completes the turnabout with the wheel going left, right, left, stopping short of each curb.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a learner permit requires passing the road test first.

correction.text: The road test is the final step for a first license and is never required for a learner permit; at renewal it may or may not be required.

prompt.text: On the backing move of a three-point turnabout, which way does Taylor turn the wheel?

answer.text: To the right, while backing up slowly.

rationale.text: Both forward moves turn the wheel left; only the backing move turns it right.

narration.text: This lesson covers the on-road driving test, the final step on the road to a first license. You will learn where the road test sits in the testing order, when it is and is not required, what you are showing the examiner, the long list of behaviors the examiner grades, and the vehicle you must bring. Then we walk step by step through the three-point turnabout, a maneuver that appears on the graded list and has a clean pattern you can memorize. The good news is that nothing on this test is exotic. It is ordinary driving, done carefully and consistently.

lines.text: After every other test is passed.
Original applicants take it, with noted exceptions.

narration.text: The on-road driving test comes last, after every other test is passed. It is required for a first license, it may be required at renewal, and it is never required for a learner permit. The handbook also states that original license applicants must take the on-road test, while noting some cases where it may not be required. So if you are getting your first North Carolina license, plan on the road test as the final gate after vision, signs and knowledge. During that test, you show that you can perform basic driving patterns and drive safely in real traffic.

Here is a trap worth practicing. Three situations, three different answers. For a learner permit, the road test is never required, because the permit is the stage where you are still learning to drive. For a first license, the road test is required and comes last. At renewal, it may or may not be required. Practice questions like to flip these, for example by claiming a permit needs a road test, or that every renewal needs one. Hold the three answers together: permit never, first license yes, renewal maybe. That one line settles most questions about when the road test applies.

lines.text: Turning, lane use, following and passing.

narration.text: Road-test examiners grade a long list of behaviors. They watch how you approach intersections, stop signs and signals, quick stops on command, backing, and stopping, starting and parking. They watch clutch use if the car is a manual, your use of turn signals and the horn, turning, lane use, following distance, passing and being passed, and yielding to pedestrians and other vehicles. They even note your posture, and they watch the three-point turnabout. The lesson here is that nearly every moment counts, so steady everyday habits matter more than any single maneuver.

lines.text: Test in a vehicle of your class.

narration.text: There is one more requirement before the test begins. You must take the driving skills test in a vehicle that represents the license class you are applying for. North Carolina issues both regular and commercial licenses, and the vehicle you will drive decides which class you need. So someone seeking an ordinary car license tests in an ordinary car, while someone seeking a heavier class tests in a vehicle of that class. The examiner is judging whether you can safely handle the kind of vehicle the license will allow, so the test vehicle has to match that class.

lines.text: Forward with the wheel turned left.
Back slowly with the wheel turned right.
Forward again with the wheel left.

narration.text: Now the turnabout, step by step. Step one: from the far right edge of the road, check for traffic, signal left, creep forward while turning the wheel left, and stop several inches from the left curb or edge. Step two: back up slowly while turning the wheel right, and stop several inches from the right curb or edge. Step three: move forward slowly with the wheel turned left to complete the turnabout. Notice that you never touch either curb; you stop several inches short each time. And notice the pattern of the wheel, which the memory line captures as left, right, left.

lines.text: Taylor is on the backing move.
Which way does the wheel turn?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: during the road test, Taylor pulls to the far right edge of a narrow street, checks traffic, signals left and creeps forward with the wheel turned left, stopping short of the left curb. Now Taylor begins the backing move. Which way should Taylor turn the wheel? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to the right, while backing up slowly and stopping several inches from the right curb or edge. Both forward moves turn the wheel left, and only the backing move turns it right. That is the left, right, left pattern in action.

lines.text: Last test, first license, never the permit.

narration.text: To finish, the on-road test comes last, after every other test is passed. It is required for a first license, may be required at renewal, and is never required for a learner permit. You take it in a vehicle that represents the license class you want, and you show basic driving patterns and safe driving in traffic. Examiners grade a long list, from intersections and backing to yielding, posture and the turnabout. For the three-point turnabout, the wheel goes left on both forward moves and right on the backing move, stopping several inches from each curb.

why_how.text: North Carolina sorts licenses by the vehicle you will drive, so knowing the class lines keeps you legal behind any wheel.
Most drivers need only a regular Class C, but the heavier regular classes use weight thresholds that are easy to mix up.

scenario.text: Chris plans to pull a large trailer rated over ten thousand pounds behind a CDL-exempt pickup for a farm hobby.

reasoning.text: The regular Class A threshold looks at the towed unit, and a towed unit rated ten thousand and one pounds or more meets it.

result.text: Chris needs a regular Class A license for that combination, not the everyday Class C.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Class C on a regular license means the same thing as commercial Class C.

correction.text: Regular and commercial classes share the letters A, B and C, but the regular Class C is the ordinary noncommercial license most car and small-truck drivers need.

prompt.text: A CDL-exempt single truck is rated at twenty-six thousand and one pounds. Which regular class does its driver need?

rationale.text: Class B covers a heavy single vehicle at that rating; Class A turns on a heavy towed unit instead.

lines.text: Most drivers need a regular Class C.

narration.text: This lesson sorts out license classes. North Carolina issues both a regular driver license and a commercial driver license, and the vehicle you will drive decides which class you need. Most people only ever need a regular Class C, the license for personal cars and small trucks. But the handbook also describes a regular Class A and a regular Class B for heavier vehicles that do not require a commercial license. You will learn what each regular class covers, how the Class A and Class B thresholds differ, and why the shared letters A, B and C can mislead you.

lines.text: Most drivers need only Class C.
Single vehicle under the twenty-six thousand line.
Towing combinations under that line, driver eighteen or older.

narration.text: Start with the license you are most likely to hold. Most drivers only need a regular Class C license for personal cars and small trucks. The regular Class C covers a noncommercial single vehicle rated under twenty-six thousand and one pounds. It also covers a towing combination rated under twenty-six thousand and one pounds combined, as long as the driver is at least eighteen. So a family car, a small pickup, or a modest trailer behind a car all fall under the regular Class C. You only step up to a heavier class when the vehicle crosses one of the higher thresholds.

lines.text: Class A: towed unit ten thousand and one pounds or more.
Class B: single vehicle twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more.

narration.text: Two regular classes sit above Class C, both for vehicles that are exempt from the commercial license. A regular Class A license covers a CDL-exempt combination whose towed unit has a gross vehicle weight rating of ten thousand and one pounds or more. A regular Class B license covers a CDL-exempt single vehicle rated at twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more, including when that vehicle tows something rated no more than ten thousand pounds. Notice where each rule looks. Class A looks at what is being towed. Class B looks at the single vehicle itself.

lines.text: Class A measures the towed unit.
Class B measures the single vehicle.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Both thresholds are about weight ratings, so they blur together. The regular Class A threshold is about the towed unit, rated ten thousand and one pounds or more. The regular Class B threshold is about a single vehicle, rated twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more. If a practice question describes a heavy trailer behind a lighter truck, think Class A. If it describes one heavy truck towing something light, think Class B. A distractor that swaps the two, putting the trailer rule on Class B, is the classic wrong answer. The memory line is short: A tows, B is heavy.

lines.text: Regular and commercial classes share letters.
CDL applicants use the CDL Handbook.
Motorcycle applicants use the Motorcycle Handbook.

narration.text: Regular license classes and commercial license classes share the letters A, B and C, and that overlap causes confusion. The regular Class C is the ordinary noncommercial license that most car and small-truck drivers need. A commercial Class C is something else, covered in the next lesson. The handbook also points other applicants to their own study material. People applying for a commercial Class A, B or C study the CDL Handbook, and people applying for a motorcycle endorsement or motorcycle permit study the Motorcycle Handbook. This handbook is the guide for the regular license.

Here is a quick check: a farm business uses a CDL-exempt single truck rated at twenty-six thousand and one pounds, and it tows nothing heavier than a small utility trailer. Which regular license class does the driver need? Work it out before reading on. The answer is regular Class B. Class B covers a CDL-exempt single vehicle rated at twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more, even when it tows something rated no more than ten thousand pounds. Class A would apply only if the towed unit itself were rated ten thousand and one pounds or more.

lines.text: Everyday drivers carry regular Class C.

narration.text: Let us recap. North Carolina issues regular and commercial licenses, and the vehicle you will drive decides the class. Most drivers need only a regular Class C, which covers noncommercial single vehicles and towing combinations rated under twenty-six thousand and one pounds, with towing allowed when the driver is at least eighteen. A regular Class A turns on a towed unit of ten thousand and one pounds or more, and a regular Class B turns on a single vehicle of twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more. Commercial and motorcycle applicants study their own handbooks.

why_how.text: A commercial license protects the public when drivers handle heavy, passenger or hazardous-cargo vehicles, whether they are paid or volunteer.
Commercial Class C is defined by what the vehicle carries, so weight alone never settles it.
Some vehicles are exempt from a CDL, but a regular license of the right class is still always required.

scenario.text: A church van is built to carry sixteen people counting the driver, and it is not a Class A or Class B vehicle.

reasoning.text: Commercial Class C covers vehicles outside Classes A and B that are built to carry sixteen or more people counting the driver.

result.text: The van falls in commercial Class C, and its driver needs a commercial license even as a volunteer.

claim.text: Many people think commercial Class C is just about weight, like the regular Class C limit.

correction.text: Commercial Class C is defined by what the vehicle carries: sixteen or more people counting the driver, or placarded hazardous materials.

prompt.text: A light delivery van carries hazardous materials that require placards. Which commercial class can it fall into?

rationale.text: Outside Classes A and B, a vehicle carrying placarded hazardous materials is a commercial Class C vehicle, whatever its weight.

lines.text: Paid or volunteer, the rule is the same.

narration.text: This lesson steps into commercial driving. Most learners will never need a commercial driver license, but the knowledge test can still ask how the classes work, and the shared letters make it easy to confuse commercial classes with regular ones. You will learn who must hold a commercial license, how commercial Class A, B and C vehicles are defined, which vehicles are exempt, how on-duty volunteer emergency drivers are treated, and which kinds of commercial driving need a special endorsement. Keep one idea in mind throughout: the vehicle and what it carries decide the license.

lines.text: Built or used for passengers or property.

narration.text: A commercial driver license is required for paid or volunteer drivers of the listed vehicle types that are built or used to carry passengers or property. That word volunteer matters. Driving without pay does not remove the requirement, so a volunteer behind the wheel of a qualifying vehicle still needs the commercial license. The requirement attaches to the kind of vehicle and its purpose, carrying passengers or property, rather than to whether the driver earns money. Practice questions often offer only paid drivers as an answer, and that option leaves out the volunteers the handbook includes.

lines.text: Class A: heavy combination, heavy towed unit.
Class B: heavy single vehicle, or light towed unit.

narration.text: Now the commercial weight classes. A commercial Class A vehicle is a combination with a combined weight rating of at least twenty-six thousand and one pounds whose towed unit is rated at least ten thousand and one pounds. A commercial Class B vehicle is a single vehicle rated at least twenty-six thousand and one pounds, or a combination whose towing unit is rated at least twenty-six thousand and one pounds while the towed unit is rated under ten thousand and one pounds. So a heavy truck pulling a heavy trailer is Class A, and a heavy truck alone or with a light trailer is Class B.

lines.text: Sixteen or more people, counting the driver.

narration.text: Here is where many learners slip. A commercial Class C vehicle is one outside Classes A and B that is built to carry sixteen or more people counting the driver, or that carries hazardous materials requiring placards. So commercial Class C is defined by what the vehicle carries, not by weight alone. That is very different from the regular Class C, which is defined by weight ratings and is the ordinary car license. If a question describes a light van with placarded cargo, or a vehicle built for sixteen riders, think commercial Class C, even though the vehicle is not heavy.

lines.text: No CDL for recreational, military or emergency equipment.
A regular license of the right class still applies.

narration.text: Some vehicles need no commercial license at all. No CDL is needed for recreational vehicles, military equipment, fire or emergency equipment, or certain farm vehicles. But a regular license of the right class is always required, so exempt never means unlicensed. A related rule covers emergency volunteers. On-duty volunteer fire, rescue or EMS members may drive Class A, B or C fire-fighting, rescue or EMS vehicles while holding only a regular A, B or C license. In other words, the volunteer still needs the matching regular class, just not the commercial version.

Beyond the class itself, certain kinds of commercial driving need a special CDL endorsement. Hauling hazardous materials, carrying passengers, driving school or activity buses, pulling double trailers and driving tank vehicles each require one. An endorsement is an extra authorization added to the commercial license for that specific kind of work. So a commercial driver who wants to haul fuel in a tank vehicle, or carry a busload of passengers, needs both the right class and the right endorsement. The memory line is simple: special loads need a special endorsement.

lines.text: A light van with placarded cargo.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a small delivery van, well under the heavy weight ratings and not part of any combination, is loaded with hazardous materials that require placards. Which commercial class can that van fall into? Work it out before reading on. The answer is commercial Class C. Outside Classes A and B, a vehicle that carries placarded hazardous materials is a commercial Class C vehicle, whatever its weight. The same is true for a vehicle built to carry sixteen or more people counting the driver. Commercial Class C is about what the vehicle carries.

lines.text: Paid or volunteer, the CDL applies.

narration.text: To finish, a commercial license is required for paid or volunteer drivers of the listed vehicles built or used to carry passengers or property. Commercial Class A is a heavy combination with a heavy towed unit, Class B is a heavy single vehicle or one with a light towed unit, and Class C is defined by sixteen or more riders or placarded hazardous materials. Recreational, military, emergency and certain farm vehicles need no CDL, though a regular license of the right class is required, and on-duty volunteers may use a regular license. Special loads need special endorsements.

why_how.text: Motorcycles need their own authorization, either a permit or an endorsement, because riding takes different skills than driving a car.
Bus drivers carry children, so the state adds age, experience, endorsements and a certificate on top of the CDL.

scenario.text: Dana, age seventeen, holds a full provisional license and wants a motorcycle learner permit.

reasoning.text: A sixteen or seventeen year old applicant must already hold a full provisional license and have a parent or guardian sign.

result.text: Dana brings a parent to sign, and the motorcycle learner permit then allows Dana to ride on public roads.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the motorcycle endorsement and the motorcycle learner permit are the same document.

correction.text: An endorsement is added to an existing regular or commercial license, while the learner permit is a separate permit; either one allows motorcycle operation.

prompt.text: Dana is seventeen with a full provisional license. What else does Dana need to apply for a motorcycle learner permit?

rationale.text: Applicants aged sixteen to seventeen need both a full provisional license and a parent or guardian signature.

lines.text: Motorcycles need a permit or endorsement.

narration.text: This last lesson in the licensing chapter covers two special groups. The first is motorcycle riders, who need a specific authorization before they can ride on public roads. The second is bus drivers, who carry students and other passengers and so face extra requirements. You will learn the two legal ways to operate a motorcycle, what a motorcycle learner permit applicant must already have at each age, how an endorsement differs from a permit, what a school bus driver needs, how an activity bus driver differs, and who is barred from the passenger and school bus endorsements.

lines.text: Or a license with a motorcycle endorsement.
Teens need a provisional license and a parent signature.

narration.text: To operate a motorcycle on public roads, a person needs one of two things: a motorcycle learner permit, or a regular or commercial license that carries a motorcycle endorsement. Getting the permit depends on age. An applicant aged sixteen to seventeen must already hold a full provisional license and have a parent or guardian sign. An applicant eighteen or older must already hold a license from the division. Notice that in both cases the motorcycle permit is not a first credential. It builds on a license the rider already has, whether provisional or full.

Here is a common trap. The motorcycle endorsement and the motorcycle learner permit are not the same document. A motorcycle endorsement is added to an existing regular or commercial license. A motorcycle learner permit is a separate permit. Either one allows motorcycle operation on public roads. Practice questions sometimes claim that only the endorsement lets you ride, or that the permit is what gets added to your license. Both claims mix up the two. Keep the picture clear: the endorsement attaches to a license you hold, and the permit stands on its own as a separate permit.

lines.text: At least eighteen with six months of experience.
Class B or C CDL with S and P endorsements.
School bus adds a driver's certificate.

narration.text: A school bus driver must be at least eighteen, have at least six months of driving experience, and hold a Class B or C commercial license with S and P endorsements, plus a School Bus Driver's Certificate. Activity bus drivers meet the same terms without the certificate, so the certificate is the difference between the two. There is also a firm bar. Under North Carolina law, the division will not issue or renew a commercial license with a P or S endorsement for anyone who must register as a sex offender. That rule protects the passengers these drivers carry.

lines.text: Dana holds a full provisional license.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dana is seventeen, already holds a full provisional license, and wants a motorcycle learner permit. What else does Dana need in order to apply? Work it out before reading on. The answer is a parent or guardian's signature. For applicants aged sixteen to seventeen, the handbook requires both a full provisional license and a parent or guardian signing. If Dana were eighteen or older, the requirement would instead be holding a license from the division. Once Dana has the permit, it is one of the two legal ways to ride on public roads.

lines.text: The certificate marks the school bus driver.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. To ride a motorcycle on public roads you need a motorcycle learner permit or a license with a motorcycle endorsement. A permit applicant aged sixteen to seventeen needs a full provisional license and a parent or guardian signature, and one eighteen or older needs a license from the division. An endorsement is added to a license, while a permit stands on its own. A school bus driver needs to be eighteen, have six months of experience, hold a Class B or C CDL with S and P endorsements, and carry the certificate that activity bus drivers do not need.
